TITLE: What Is a Diffusion Model? How AI Image and Video Generators Work
LABEL: EXPLAINER
EXCERPT: Diffusion models create images, video and audio by starting from random noise and removing it step by step. A plain-English explanation of how Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Midjourney and Sora-style models work, latent diffusion, guidance, samplers, transformers and the GPUs they need.
KEY: A diffusion model is a type of generative AI that creates images, video or audio by starting from pure random noise and removing that noise step by step until a clear result appears, guided by your text prompt. It learns this by training on millions of images that were gradually corrupted with noise and learning to undo the damage. Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Midjourney, DALL-E 3 and AI video models such as Sora and Veo are all built on diffusion or its close relative, flow matching.
content:
Short answer

A diffusion model is a type of generative AI that creates images, video or audio by starting from pure random noise and removing that noise step by step until a clear result appears, guided by your text prompt. It learns this by training on millions of images that were gradually corrupted with noise and learning to undo the damage. Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Midjourney, DALL-E 3 and AI video models such as Sora and Veo are all built on diffusion or its close relative, flow matching.

The idea in plain English

Imagine taking a photo and adding a little static, then a little more, hundreds of times, until it is nothing but grey noise. That is easy. Now imagine learning to run the process backwards: looking at a noisy image and guessing what a slightly cleaner version would look like. Do that enough times and you can start from pure noise and end up with a brand-new, sharp image.

A diffusion model is a neural network trained to do exactly that reverse step.

How diffusion models work

Training: learning to remove noise

1. Take a real image and its caption from the training set. 2. Add a random amount of Gaussian noise to the image. 3. Ask the network to predict the noise that was added (or, in newer methods, the direction back to the clean image), given the noisy image, the noise level and the caption. 4. Compare the prediction with the truth and adjust the network's weights.

Repeated over hundreds of millions of image-caption pairs, the model learns what images look like and how words relate to visual features.

Generation: from noise to picture

1. Start with an image made of pure random noise. 2. The model predicts the noise in it, using your prompt as guidance. 3. A sampler (scheduler) removes part of that noise. 4. Repeat for typically 20 to 50 steps (fewer with distilled "turbo" models). 5. Decode the result into the final image.

Because the starting noise is random, the same prompt gives a different image each time unless you fix the seed.

Key ideas that made diffusion practical

Latent diffusion

Running diffusion on full-resolution pixels is very expensive. Latent diffusion, introduced in 2021 and used by Stable Diffusion, first compresses images with an autoencoder (VAE) into a much smaller latent representation, runs diffusion there, then decodes back to pixels. This cut compute enough to run on consumer GPUs.

Text conditioning

A text encoder (such as CLIP or T5) turns your prompt into embeddings. The denoising network attends to those embeddings at every step, which is how the words steer the picture. The mechanism is the same attention used in language models.

Classifier-free guidance (CFG)

The model makes two predictions each step, one with your prompt and one without, and pushes the result further towards the prompted version. The CFG scale setting controls how strictly the image follows the prompt: higher values follow it more closely but can look oversaturated.

From U-Nets to transformers

Early diffusion models used a convolutional U-Net. Newer models such as Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX and most video models use diffusion transformers (DiT), the same transformer architecture behind LLMs, which scales better with more data and compute.

Flow matching

Many recent models are trained with flow matching or rectified flow, a closely related approach that learns straighter paths from noise to image. This allows good results in fewer steps. FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 use it.

What diffusion models are used for

  • Image generation: Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Midjourney, DALL-E 3, Imagen.
  • Image editing: inpainting (replace part of an image), outpainting (extend it), style transfer, upscaling.
  • Video: text-to-video and image-to-video models such as Sora, Veo, Kling and the open Wan models.
  • Audio and music: speech, sound effects and music generation.
  • Science: protein design, molecule generation and weather forecasting.
  • Text (experimental): "diffusion language models" generate whole blocks of text in parallel instead of one token at a time.

Diffusion models vs LLMs vs GANs

For the bigger picture, see What is generative AI?.

What hardware diffusion models need

Diffusion is mostly compute-bound: each step runs the whole network over the full latent image, so GPU TFLOPS and tensor cores matter more than they do for chatbots, where speed is limited mainly by memory bandwidth. VRAM still decides which models fit:

Our best GPU for Stable Diffusion guide covers which cards to buy, and the GPU cloud price tracker shows what it costs to rent data center GPUs for heavier jobs.

Common settings explained

  • Steps: more steps can add detail but take longer; 20 to 30 is typical.
  • CFG / guidance scale: how strongly to follow the prompt.
  • Sampler: the algorithm that removes noise (Euler, DPM++ and others).
  • Seed: the starting noise; reuse it to reproduce an image.
  • Negative prompt: what you do not want (supported by some models).
  • LoRA: a small add-on that teaches a style or subject, the same idea as LoRA fine-tuning for LLMs.

Frequently asked questions

Why is it called diffusion?

The name comes from physics, where diffusion describes particles spreading out, like ink in water. Adding noise to an image step by step is mathematically similar, and the model learns to reverse it.

Is Midjourney a diffusion model?

Midjourney has not published its architecture in detail, but it is widely understood to be diffusion-based, like most leading image generators.

Why do AI images sometimes have wrong hands or text?

Hands and lettering have precise structures that are easy to get slightly wrong when generating from noise. Larger, newer models with better text encoders have greatly improved both.

Can I run a diffusion model on my own computer?

Yes. Stable Diffusion and FLUX run locally through apps like ComfyUI or Forge on an NVIDIA GPU with 8 GB or more, ideally 16 GB.

Sources and further reading

  • Ho et al., Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (2020)
  • Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (2021)
  • Ho and Salimans, Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance (2022)
  • Peebles and Xie, Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (2022)
  • Lipman et al., Flow Matching for Generative Modeling (2022)

TITLE: What Is a GPU? Graphics Processing Units Explained Simply (and Why AI Needs Them)
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor with thousands of small cores that do many calculations at once. What a GPU does, GPU vs CPU, integrated vs dedicated graphics, VRAM, why GPUs power AI, the main makers and how to choose one.
KEY: A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor built to perform thousands of simple calculations at the same time. It was originally designed to draw 3D graphics for games, which means calculating millions of pixels in parallel. That same ability makes GPUs ideal for artificial intelligence, video editing and scientific computing. A CPU has a handful of powerful cores for general tasks; a GPU has thousands of smaller cores plus its own fast memory (VRAM), and modern GPUs add tensor cores built specifically for AI math.
content:
Short answer

A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor built to perform thousands of simple calculations at the same time. It was originally designed to draw 3D graphics for games, which means calculating millions of pixels in parallel. That same ability makes GPUs ideal for artificial intelligence, video editing and scientific computing. A CPU has a handful of powerful cores for general tasks; a GPU has thousands of smaller cores plus its own fast memory (VRAM), and modern GPUs add tensor cores built specifically for AI math.

What does a GPU do?

Every frame you see in a game is made of millions of pixels, and each one needs its colour, lighting and position calculated, 60 or more times per second. Those calculations are similar and independent, so they can be done side by side. A GPU is built for exactly this kind of parallel work.

Today GPUs are used for:

  • Gaming and 3D graphics: rendering scenes, lighting, ray tracing and upscaling such as DLSS.
  • Artificial intelligence: training and running neural networks, from chatbots to image generators.
  • Video: editing, effects, encoding and streaming.
  • Science and engineering: simulations of weather, molecules, fluids and physics.
  • Data analysis: speeding up large database queries and data science workloads.
  • Displaying your screen: every computer needs some form of GPU to output an image.

GPU vs CPU

The CPU and GPU work together: the CPU runs the program and hands the heavy parallel maths to the GPU. For a deeper comparison, read GPU vs CPU for AI.

Integrated vs dedicated GPUs

  • Integrated GPU: built into the processor chip and shares system memory. Found in most laptops and office PCs, and in phones. Fine for everyday use, video and light games. Apple Silicon Macs use a powerful integrated GPU with large shared "unified memory".
  • Dedicated (discrete) GPU: a separate graphics card or chip with its own VRAM and cooling. Needed for serious gaming, 3D work and most local AI.
  • Data center GPUs: chips like the NVIDIA H100, H200 and B200 or AMD Instinct MI300X, built for AI and supercomputers, with huge memory and no display outputs.

What is inside a GPU?

  • Streaming multiprocessors (SMs): the building blocks that hold the cores. Explained in how a GPU works.
  • CUDA cores (NVIDIA) or stream processors (AMD): general arithmetic units. See What are CUDA cores?.
  • Tensor cores: specialised units for the matrix multiplications at the heart of AI. See tensor cores vs CUDA cores.
  • RT cores: hardware for ray-traced lighting in games. See tensor cores vs RT cores.
  • VRAM: the GPU's own fast memory (GDDR7 on consumer cards, HBM on data center chips). See What is VRAM?.
  • Memory bus and bandwidth: how fast data flows between VRAM and the cores. See GPU memory bandwidth.

Why AI runs on GPUs

Neural networks are mostly giant matrix multiplications: multiplying large grids of numbers together, billions of times. That work is massively parallel, just like graphics. Three moments made GPUs the engine of the AI boom:

1. 2007: CUDA. NVIDIA released CUDA, letting programmers use GPUs for general computing, not just graphics. See What is CUDA?. 2. 2012: AlexNet. A neural network trained on two NVIDIA GTX 580 gaming GPUs won the ImageNet image-recognition contest by a wide margin, kick-starting the deep learning era. 3. 2017: tensor cores. NVIDIA's Volta V100 added tensor cores dedicated to AI maths, multiplying AI performance.

Today's large language models are trained on clusters of thousands of data center GPUs (see What is a GPU cluster?), and every ChatGPT-style answer is generated on GPUs or similar AI chips.

Who makes GPUs?

  • NVIDIA: GeForce for gaming, RTX PRO for workstations, and H100/H200/B200-class chips that dominate AI data centers.
  • AMD: Radeon for gaming and Instinct accelerators for AI and supercomputing. See AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.
  • Intel: Arc graphics cards and integrated graphics.
  • Apple, Qualcomm and Arm-based chipmakers: integrated GPUs in Macs, phones and tablets.

Google's TPUs and other AI accelerators are not GPUs, but they compete with GPUs for AI work. See NPU vs GPU vs TPU.

How to choose a GPU

  • For everyday use and office work: an integrated GPU is enough.
  • For gaming: match the GPU to your monitor resolution and refresh rate.
  • For video editing and 3D: more VRAM and strong encoders help.
  • For AI: VRAM decides which models you can run; memory bandwidth decides how fast. 16 GB is a good minimum for local AI. See best GPU for local LLMs and best GPU for Stable Diffusion.
  • For big AI jobs: renting is often cheaper than buying; compare today's prices in our GPU cloud price tracker.

To compare models in detail, learn how to read a GPU spec sheet.

Frequently asked questions

Is a GPU the same as a graphics card?

Not quite. The GPU is the chip itself. A graphics card is the whole board that holds the GPU, its VRAM, power delivery, cooling and display outputs.

Does my computer have a GPU?

Yes. Every computer that shows an image has a GPU, either integrated into the processor or as a separate card. On Windows, open Task Manager and look under Performance to see it.

Why are GPUs so expensive?

Demand from AI data centers, gaming and crypto has repeatedly outpaced supply, and high-end GPUs use advanced, costly chip manufacturing and memory. See why GPU prices are rising.

What was the first GPU?

NVIDIA marketed its GeForce 256, released in 1999, as the world's first GPU, because it moved 3D transform and lighting calculations from the CPU onto the graphics chip.

Sources and further reading

  • NVIDIA, GeForce RTX 5090 specifications
  • NVIDIA, CUDA Zone
  • Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (AlexNet, 2012)
  • NVIDIA, NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU Architecture whitepaper (2017)

TITLE: What Is a Small Language Model (SLM)? SLM vs LLM, Examples and When to Use One
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Small language models (SLMs) are compact AI models, usually from under 1 to around 10 billion parameters, that run fast and cheaply on laptops, phones and single GPUs. SLM vs LLM, popular examples like Phi, Gemma, Llama and Qwen, how they are made, and what hardware they need.
KEY: A small language model (SLM) is a language model with relatively few parameters, typically from under 1 billion to around 10 billion, compared with hundreds of billions or more for frontier large language models. SLMs are cheaper, faster and private: they can run on a laptop, phone, AI PC or a single GPU. They are less capable on broad, complex reasoning, but for focused tasks such as classification, extraction, summarising or powering an app feature, a well-trained or fine-tuned SLM can match much larger models at a fraction of the cost.
content:
Short answer

A small language model (SLM) is a language model with relatively few parameters, typically from under 1 billion to around 10 billion, compared with hundreds of billions or more for frontier large language models. SLMs are cheaper, faster and private: they can run on a laptop, phone, AI PC or a single GPU. They are less capable on broad, complex reasoning, but for focused tasks such as classification, extraction, summarising or powering an app feature, a well-trained or fine-tuned SLM can match much larger models at a fraction of the cost.

SLM vs LLM

There is no official cut-off, but this is how the terms are generally used:

For background on how both work, see What is an LLM?.

Popular small language models

How small models got so good

  • Better data: Microsoft's Phi research showed that carefully filtered "textbook quality" and synthetic data lets small models punch far above their size.
  • Knowledge distillation: a small "student" model learns to imitate a large "teacher" model's outputs, inheriting much of its ability.
  • Over-training: small models are now trained on many trillions of tokens, far more than older scaling rules suggested, which improves quality per parameter.
  • Pruning: removing less important weights and layers from a larger model, then retraining briefly.
  • Quantization: storing weights in 4 or 8 bits shrinks memory with little quality loss. See LLM quantization.
  • Fine-tuning: a small model fine-tuned on one task can beat a general large model on that task.

When to use a small language model

Good fits:

  • On-device features: autocomplete, smart replies, summarising notifications, offline assistants.
  • Privacy-sensitive data: medical, legal or company documents that should not leave your hardware.
  • High-volume, simple tasks: classifying tickets, extracting fields, tagging content, routing requests.
  • Low latency: real-time features where every millisecond counts.
  • Cost control: millions of requests per day at near-zero marginal cost.
  • Agents: many steps in an AI agent workflow are routine (formatting, tool calls) and can use an SLM, saving the large model for hard decisions.
  • RAG systems: with good retrieval, a small model can answer accurately from your documents. See What is RAG?.

Use a large model instead for open-ended research, complex coding, long multi-step reasoning, broad world knowledge and high-stakes writing.

Hardware for small language models

SLMs are where local AI shines:

Generation speed depends mainly on memory bandwidth, so even a mid-range GPU can produce more than 100 tokens per second with a 3B to 8B model. NPUs in phones and AI PCs run the smallest models with very low power. For exact numbers for your setup, use our VRAM guide, and to get started see how to run an LLM locally.

Frequently asked questions

How small is a "small" language model?

Most people mean models under roughly 10 billion parameters, but the line moves as hardware improves. Some include models up to about 14 billion parameters that fit on a single consumer GPU.

Are small language models as good as ChatGPT?

Not for everything. Frontier models are much stronger at broad knowledge and complex reasoning. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a good SLM, especially a fine-tuned one, can be close or equal.

Can I run an SLM without a GPU?

Yes. Models of 1B to 4B parameters run acceptably on a modern CPU or Apple Silicon, and on phones. A GPU makes them much faster.

Are SLMs safer for private data?

Running a model locally keeps data on your own device, which avoids sending it to a cloud provider. You still need normal security practices for the device and application.

Sources and further reading

  • Abdin et al., Phi-3 Technical Report: A Highly Capable Language Model Locally on Your Phone (2024)
  • Gunasekar et al., Textbooks Are All You Need (2023)
  • Hinton et al., Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network (2015)
  • Google, Gemma models documentation
  • Hugging Face, SmolLM

TITLE: What Is MCP (Model Context Protocol)? How AI Connects to Tools and Data
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI assistants connect to tools, apps and data through one common interface. How MCP works, hosts, clients and servers, tools vs resources vs prompts, real examples and security risks.
KEY: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data, such as files, databases, GitHub, Slack or a web browser. Instead of building a custom integration for every app and every AI model, a developer writes one MCP server, and any MCP-compatible AI app can use it. Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024; OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and many developer tools have since adopted it, which is why it is often called the "USB-C port for AI".
content:
Short answer

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data, such as files, databases, GitHub, Slack or a web browser. Instead of building a custom integration for every app and every AI model, a developer writes one MCP server, and any MCP-compatible AI app can use it. Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024; OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and many developer tools have since adopted it, which is why it is often called the "USB-C port for AI".

Why MCP exists

A large language model on its own only knows what was in its training data and can only produce text. To be useful at work, it needs to read your documents, query a database, create a calendar event or open a pull request. Before MCP, every AI app needed its own custom connector for every service. With M AI apps and N services, that meant building and maintaining up to M × N integrations.

MCP turns that into M + N: each service exposes one MCP server, each AI app implements one MCP client, and they can all talk to each other.

How MCP works

MCP uses a simple client-server design built on JSON-RPC 2.0 messages.

A typical flow:

1. The host starts and connects to the configured MCP servers. 2. Each server tells the client what it offers. 3. You ask a question, for example "Summarise the open bugs in our repo". 4. The model sees the available tools, decides to call one (such as list_issues) and the client sends the request to the server. 5. The server runs the action and returns the result, which is added to the model's context window. 6. The model writes its answer using the real data.

Servers can run locally (started by the host and connected over standard input/output) or remotely over HTTP, which lets companies host MCP servers for their products.

The three building blocks: tools, resources and prompts

  • Tools are actions the model can call: search the web, run a SQL query, send a message, create a file. The model decides when to use them, usually with user approval.
  • Resources are data the app can read and add to context: files, documents, database records, API responses.
  • Prompts are reusable templates a server provides, such as "review this pull request" or "draft a release note".

This makes MCP the plumbing behind many AI agents: the agent plans, and MCP gives it hands.

What people use MCP for

  • Coding: letting an AI assistant read a repository, run tests, check CI and open pull requests.
  • Company knowledge: searching Google Drive, Notion, Confluence or SharePoint and answering with sources, a live alternative to building your own RAG pipeline.
  • Data analysis: querying databases and spreadsheets directly instead of copying data into a chat.
  • Productivity: reading email and calendars, creating tasks, posting updates.
  • Browser and desktop automation: controlling a browser to fill forms or test a website.
  • Design and content: connecting AI to design tools, CMSs and analytics.

MCP vs function calling vs plugins

MCP does not replace function calling; it builds on it. The model still uses function calling to request a tool, and MCP standardises how that request reaches the tool.

Who supports MCP?

Anthropic open-sourced MCP in November 2024 with SDKs and reference servers. During 2025, OpenAI added MCP support to its Agents SDK and ChatGPT, Google announced support for Gemini, and Microsoft built MCP into GitHub Copilot, VS Code and Windows. In December 2025, Anthropic donated MCP to a new Linux Foundation project, the Agentic AI Foundation, so it is governed as a neutral open standard. Thousands of community and official servers now exist for popular services.

Security risks to know

Connecting AI to real systems brings real risks:

  • Prompt injection: text inside a web page, email or document can contain hidden instructions that try to make the model misuse its tools.
  • Over-broad permissions: a server with write access to everything can do a lot of damage if the model is tricked or makes a mistake.
  • Untrusted servers: a malicious MCP server can describe its tools misleadingly or leak data.
  • Data exposure: results returned by tools go into the model's context and may be logged.

Good practice: install servers only from trusted sources, grant the least access needed, require confirmation for actions such as sending, deleting or paying, and review what each tool does. This is part of the wider AI alignment and safety challenge of giving models more autonomy.

How to start using MCP

1. As a user: open your AI app's settings (for example Claude Desktop, ChatGPT or your code editor), find the connectors or MCP section, and add a server such as file system, GitHub or a database. 2. As a developer: use an official SDK (Python, TypeScript and others) to write a server that exposes a few tools, then connect it to a host for testing.

A minimal Python server looks like this:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("gpu-prices")

@mcp.tool()
def h100_price() -> str:
    """Return today's typical H100 cloud price per GPU-hour."""
    return "See https://tensorcore.si/gpu-cloud-pricing/ for live prices"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

Frequently asked questions

Is MCP only for Claude?

No. Anthropic created it, but MCP is an open standard supported by many AI apps and models, including products from OpenAI, Google and Microsoft, and open-source tools.

Do I need to code to use MCP?

No. Many apps let you add ready-made MCP servers or connectors from a settings menu. Coding is only needed to build your own server.

Is MCP the same as an API?

MCP usually sits on top of existing APIs. An MCP server wraps a service's API and describes it in a standard way that AI models can discover and use.

Does MCP make AI hallucinate less?

It can, because the model can fetch real data instead of guessing. But the model can still misread results, so important outputs should be checked. See AI hallucinations.

Sources and further reading

  • Anthropic, Introducing the Model Context Protocol (November 2024)
  • Anthropic, Donating the Model Context Protocol and establishing the Agentic AI Foundation (December 2025)
  • Model Context Protocol documentation and specification
  • Model Context Protocol on GitHub

TITLE: What Is Multimodal AI? How Models See, Hear and Talk (With Examples)
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Multimodal AI models understand and generate more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio and video. How multimodal models like GPT-4o and Gemini work, image tokens and vision encoders, real uses, limits and the hardware they need.
KEY: Multimodal AI is artificial intelligence that can understand and work with several types of data at once, such as text, images, audio, video and documents. A multimodal model can read a photo of a receipt and total it, describe a chart, answer questions about a video, or hold a spoken conversation. Leading examples include OpenAI's GPT-4o and later models, Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude. Most work by converting every input into tokens that a single transformer can process together.
content:
Short answer

Multimodal AI is artificial intelligence that can understand and work with several types of data at once, such as text, images, audio, video and documents. A multimodal model can read a photo of a receipt and total it, describe a chart, answer questions about a video, or hold a spoken conversation. Leading examples include OpenAI's GPT-4o and later models, Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude. Most work by converting every input into tokens that a single transformer can process together.

What "modality" means

A modality is a type of data: text, images, audio, video, and also less obvious ones such as sensor readings, 3D data or code. Early AI systems handled one modality each: a language model for text, a separate vision model for images, a separate speech recogniser for audio.

A multimodal model combines them. That matters because the real world is multimodal: a doctor looks at scans and reads notes, a mechanic listens to an engine and reads error codes, and you might want to ask a question about a screenshot.

Types of multimodal AI

How multimodal models work

1. Encoders turn each modality into vectors

Images are cut into small patches (for example 14 × 14 or 16 × 16 pixels), and a vision encoder, often a vision transformer trained with methods like CLIP, turns each patch into a vector. Audio is split into short frames and encoded the same way. These vectors are embeddings in the same kind of space the language model uses for words.

2. Everything becomes tokens

The image and audio embeddings are projected into the language model's input space, so to the model they look like extra tokens alongside your text. One image can become hundreds to a few thousand tokens depending on resolution.

3. One transformer reasons over all of it

A single transformer uses attention across all tokens, so the words in your question can "look at" the relevant parts of the image. That is how it can answer "what is the price on the second line of this receipt?"

4. Decoders produce non-text outputs

To generate images or speech, the model outputs special tokens that a decoder turns into pixels or audio, or it hands off to a dedicated generator such as a diffusion model.

Natively multimodal vs pipelines

Older voice assistants chained three separate models: speech-to-text, a text LLM, then text-to-speech. That loses tone and emotion and adds delay. Natively multimodal models such as GPT-4o (May 2024) and Gemini (trained on multiple modalities from the start) process audio and images directly, which enables faster, more natural voice conversations and better visual understanding.

Real-world uses

  • Document AI: reading scanned PDFs, forms, invoices, tables and handwriting.
  • Customer support: users send a photo of a broken product or an error screen.
  • Accessibility: describing images and surroundings for blind and low-vision users.
  • Education: photographing a maths problem and getting a step-by-step explanation.
  • Healthcare research: combining images, notes and lab results (with careful validation).
  • Retail: visual search ("find shoes like these").
  • Robotics and self-driving: combining camera, lidar and language instructions.
  • Agents: AI agents that look at screenshots to operate websites and apps.
  • Content creation: generating images, video, voice-overs and music from text.

Limitations

  • Visual mistakes: models can misread small text, count objects wrongly or misjudge spatial positions.
  • Hallucinations: a model may describe things that are not in the image. See AI hallucinations.
  • Cost and speed: images and video use many tokens, which fills the context window and raises cost.
  • Privacy: photos and recordings often contain personal information.
  • Deepfakes: realistic generated images, voices and video can be misused.

What hardware multimodal AI needs

Multimodal inputs make prompts much longer. A few high-resolution images or a minute of video can add thousands of tokens, which increases the KV cache and the time to process the prompt (the compute-heavy prefill phase). Vision encoders add their own compute too. In practice:

  • Cloud models run on data center GPUs with large HBM memory.
  • Local vision models such as Llama 3.2 Vision, Qwen2.5-VL or Gemma 3 run on consumer GPUs; plan for a few extra GB of VRAM beyond the text-only model. See how much VRAM you need.
  • On-device multimodal features on phones and AI PCs use NPUs with small, efficient models.

Frequently asked questions

Is ChatGPT multimodal?

Yes. ChatGPT can take images, files and voice as input and can produce images and speech, using OpenAI's multimodal models.

What is the difference between multimodal AI and generative AI?

Generative AI creates new content; multimodal AI handles multiple data types. Many modern systems are both, but a text-only chatbot is generative without being multimodal, and an image classifier that reads captions is multimodal without being generative. See What is generative AI?.

What is a vision language model (VLM)?

A VLM is a multimodal model that takes images and text as input and produces text. It is the most common type of multimodal model today.

Can I run a multimodal model locally?

Yes. Tools such as Ollama and LM Studio support open vision models. A GPU with 12 to 24 GB of VRAM handles most small and mid-sized ones. See how to run an LLM locally.

Sources and further reading

  • Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP, 2021)
  • Dosovitskiy et al., An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale (2020)
  • Liu et al., Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA, 2023)
  • OpenAI, Hello GPT-4o (May 2024)
  • Google, Gemini: A Family of Highly Capable Multimodal Models (2023)

TITLE: What Is Prompt Engineering? 12 Techniques That Get Better AI Answers (With Examples)
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Prompt engineering is the skill of writing instructions that get accurate, useful results from AI models like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. 12 proven techniques with before-and-after examples, templates, and how prompting compares with RAG and fine-tuning.
KEY: Prompt engineering is the practice of writing and structuring instructions for an AI model so it gives accurate, useful and consistent answers. The most effective techniques are simple: be specific about the goal, give context and examples, say what format you want, break big tasks into steps, and let the model think before it answers. Good prompting is the cheapest way to improve AI results, and it should be tried before RAG or fine-tuning.
content:
Short answer

Prompt engineering is the practice of writing and structuring instructions for an AI model so it gives accurate, useful and consistent answers. The most effective techniques are simple: be specific about the goal, give context and examples, say what format you want, break big tasks into steps, and let the model think before it answers. Good prompting is the cheapest way to improve AI results, and it should be tried before RAG or fine-tuning.

Why prompts matter

A large language model generates text by predicting what is most likely to come next given everything in its context window. Your prompt is the main thing that shapes that prediction. A vague prompt leaves the model guessing about your audience, purpose, length and format, so it falls back on generic answers. A clear prompt removes the guesswork.

A useful mental model: write the prompt as if you were briefing a smart new colleague who knows nothing about your project.

12 prompt engineering techniques

1. Be specific about the task

  • Weak: "Write about GPUs."
  • Better: "Write a 300-word explanation of why GPUs are faster than CPUs for training neural networks, for readers with no technical background."

2. Give context and the reason behind the request

Explain who the output is for and why. "This summary will go to our finance team to decide whether to rent or buy GPUs" leads to a very different answer than a bare "summarise this".

3. Assign a role

"You are an experienced data center hardware engineer" helps the model choose the right vocabulary, depth and priorities. Roles work best combined with specific instructions.

4. Show examples (few-shot prompting)

Give one to five examples of the input and the output you want. Models copy patterns very well, so examples are often the fastest way to get a consistent style or format.

Classify each GPU as "data center" or "consumer".
H100 -> data center
RTX 4090 -> consumer
B200 ->

5. Specify the output format

Ask for exactly what you need: a table with named columns, a bulleted list, JSON with specific keys, or a maximum length. "Return JSON with keys name, vram_gb and price_usd" is far more reliable than "give me the data".

6. Separate instructions from content

When you paste a document, mark clearly where it starts and ends, for example with XML-style tags: <document> ... </document>. This stops the model confusing your material with your instructions.

7. Let the model think step by step

For maths, logic, coding and analysis, ask the model to reason before answering ("Work through this step by step, then give the final answer"). This chain-of-thought approach improves accuracy on multi-step problems. Reasoning models do this automatically.

8. Break complex tasks into steps

Instead of one giant prompt, chain smaller ones: first extract the key facts, then outline, then draft, then check. Each step is easier for the model and easier for you to verify.

9. Tell it what to do, not only what to avoid

"Write in short, plain sentences" works better than "Don't be wordy". Positive instructions give the model a target.

10. Allow "I don't know"

Add "If the answer is not in the provided text, say you don't know." This reduces hallucinations, especially when answering from documents.

11. Ask for sources or quotes

"Quote the sentence from the document that supports each claim" makes answers easier to check and keeps the model grounded.

12. Iterate

Treat the first answer as a draft. Tell the model what to change ("make it shorter", "add a comparison table", "the tone is too formal") rather than starting over. Save prompts that work well as templates.

A reusable prompt template

Role: You are a [expert type].
Task: [What you want, in one or two sentences].
Context: [Who it is for, why it matters, background].
Input: <material> [paste text, data or code] </material>
Requirements:
- [Length, tone, audience]
- [Must include / must avoid]
Output format: [table / bullets / JSON with keys ...]
If information is missing, say so instead of guessing.

Prompting for different tasks

For image models such as Stable Diffusion and FLUX, prompts describe the scene and style instead of giving instructions. See What is a diffusion model?.

Prompt engineering vs RAG vs fine-tuning

Start with prompting. Add RAG when the model lacks knowledge, and fine-tuning when you need behaviour that prompting cannot deliver reliably.

From prompt engineering to context engineering

As AI moves from single questions to AI agents that work for many steps, practitioners increasingly talk about context engineering: deciding everything the model sees, including instructions, retrieved documents, tool results, memory and examples, and keeping that context relevant and within limits. Tools connected through MCP are part of that context too.

Frequently asked questions

Is prompt engineering still useful with smarter models?

Yes. Newer models need fewer tricks, but they still cannot read your mind. Clear goals, context, examples and output formats remain the biggest drivers of quality.

Is prompt engineering a real job?

Some companies hired dedicated prompt engineers when generative AI took off. Today it is more often a core skill for developers, writers, analysts and anyone who works with AI, rather than a separate role.

Do long prompts work better?

Longer is better only when it adds relevant detail. Irrelevant text can distract the model and costs more tokens.

Do prompts work the same on ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini?

The core techniques work across all major models, but each responds a little differently. Test important prompts on the model you will actually use.

  • Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (2022)

content:
Short answer

Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want in plain language to an AI model and letting it write, run and fix the code, with the human guiding by results ("make the button bigger", "it crashes when I log in") rather than reading every line. The term was coined by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy in February 2025 and was named Collins Dictionary's Word of the Year for 2025. It is great for prototypes and personal tools, but risky for production software unless someone reviews the code.

Where the term came from

On February 2, 2025, Andrej Karpathy, a co-founder of OpenAI and former head of AI at Tesla, posted about a new way of programming where you "fully give in to the vibes" and forget the code even exists. He described accepting AI changes without reading the diffs, pasting error messages back to the AI and letting it fix them.

The phrase spread quickly because it captured something real: large language models had become good enough that non-programmers could build working apps, and professional developers could build far faster. By November 2025, Collins Dictionary had picked "vibe coding" as its Word of the Year.

How vibe coding works

1. Describe the goal: "Build a web page that shows today's GPU cloud prices in a sortable table." 2. Let the AI build it: an AI coding tool writes the files, installs packages and runs the app. 3. Test by using it: you click around and see what works. 4. Give feedback in plain words: "The prices should be in dollars per hour" or paste the error message. 5. Repeat until it does what you want.

Modern tools work as AI agents: they can read the whole project, run commands and tests, browse documentation and fix their own mistakes in a loop. Many connect to services like GitHub or databases through MCP.

Popular vibe coding tools

Vibe coding vs AI-assisted programming

Not all AI-assisted coding is vibe coding. Developer Simon Willison and others draw a useful line:

Professional teams increasingly use AI for most of the typing while engineers still review, test and take responsibility for what ships.

What vibe coding is good for

  • Prototypes and MVPs: test an idea in hours instead of weeks.
  • Personal tools: a budget tracker, a file renamer, a dashboard for your own data.
  • Internal tools: simple admin panels or reports that only a few people use.
  • Learning: seeing working code for an idea, then asking the AI to explain it.
  • Websites and landing pages: fast first versions that a designer or developer can refine.
  • Data analysis: quick scripts to clean a spreadsheet or draw a chart.

The risks of vibe coding

  • Security holes: AI-generated code can include injection flaws, exposed API keys, missing authentication or weak database permissions. Several vibe-coded apps have leaked user data because nobody checked access rules.
  • Hidden bugs: code that works in a demo can fail with real users, edge cases or larger data.
  • Maintainability: a large codebase nobody understands becomes hard to change; the AI may also struggle once the project grows beyond what fits in its context window.
  • Hallucinated libraries and APIs: models sometimes call packages or functions that do not exist, and attackers have registered fake package names to exploit this. See AI hallucinations.
  • Costs: agents running many steps consume a lot of tokens, and cloud services the app uses can generate surprise bills.
  • Licensing and compliance: you are still responsible for the code you publish.

How to vibe code more safely

  • Keep secrets (API keys, passwords) out of code and out of chats; use environment variables.
  • Ask the AI to add tests, then run them.
  • Ask a second pass to review the code for security issues, or have a developer review anything that handles user data or payments.
  • Use version control (Git) so you can undo bad changes.
  • Start small, commit often, and keep the project structure simple.
  • Turn on authentication and database access rules before sharing an app publicly.

Does vibe coding need special hardware?

No. Most vibe coding tools run on cloud models, so any laptop works. If you want privacy or to avoid usage costs, you can run open coding models locally, but good coding models need plenty of VRAM: a 24 to 32 GB GPU or a high-memory Mac handles mid-sized models well. See how to run an LLM locally and the best GPU for local LLMs.

Frequently asked questions

Can someone with no coding experience vibe code?

Yes. Browser-based app builders let beginners create working web apps from descriptions. Understanding basic concepts (what a database, API and login are) helps a lot when something goes wrong.

Will vibe coding replace programmers?

It is changing the job more than removing it. AI writes more of the code, while engineers spend more time on design, review, testing, security and deciding what to build. Complex, reliable systems still need people who understand them.

Is vibe coding good for learning to code?

It can be, if you ask the AI to explain what it wrote and you experiment with changes. Accepting code blindly teaches little.

Which AI model is best for vibe coding?

The leading coding models change often. Frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are the most capable today, and reasoning modes help with harder bugs. See What is a reasoning model?.

Sources and further reading

  • Euronews, Vibe coding named word of the year by Collins Dictionary (November 2025)
  • Simon Willison, Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding (March 2025)
  • Wikipedia, Vibe coding
